statement: Here's an AI model that has to read about 128,000 tokens of Sherlock Holmes novels before it can answer a single question.
And that takes it a little over 19 seconds.
And here's the exact same model with the exact same books, except this time the whole pile was squeezed down into just 16 tokens, and it answered in about 3 seconds.
And no matter how many more documents you add, the model itself only ever reads those 16 tokens.
Now, how can a model answer questions about a whole pile of books from just 16 tokens?

Well, this is a new research project from Stanford called Memorilla, and it claims that it can squeeze a whole conversation of documents like your entire chat history or a full book into just 16 so-called memory tokens.
A language model can only use what fits into its prompt, which is called the context window.

So the way it works is that first an embedding model turns every document into a single vector and then a small trained memory module looks at all of those vectors together with your question and compresses them into 16 memory tokens and then a normal unmodified language model which in this case is quen 3 reads those 16 tokens instead of the actual text.
So, those 16 memory tokens are actually 16 vectors, and they get plugged directly into Quinn 3's input in the same spot where the embeddings of normal words would usually go.
all it's around 200 million parameters by my count.
And basically it starts with 16 learned slots which first look at your question and then go through all of your document vectors.
So basically each slot gives every document a score for how relevant it is to the question and then it blends the documents together learning mostly on the ones that scored the highest.
And it does that twice so the second pass can refine what the first one picked up.
And what's nice about the setup is that Quen 3 and the embedding model stay frozen the whole time.
The researchers trained it in three stages.
First they taught it to reconstruct around 2 million Wikipedia passages.
Then they trained it on a mix of question and answering and summarization data sets.
Memorila always hands the model the same 16 tokens, however big your history gets.
And on one factchecking benchmark, it was even more accurate than giving a model every single document.
They also reported that on one H00 GPU, the answering speed stayed at about 0.74 seconds.
And even with a context of 512 documents while putting everything in the prompt took almost 20 seconds.
So for these tests, I spun up the same H100 GPU in the cloud, similar to the conditions they had in their tests.
So, in their own example, a user has 107 old chats with an assistant, which is about 32,000 tokens, and the assistant asks for some easy breakfast ideas that will keep them full all morning.
The plain quen 3 model gives the usual list of oatmeal and yogurt recommendations, but Memorilla starts its answer with since you've got a family history of type 2 diabetes.
There was just one chat where they asked whether diabetes on your mother's side raises your risk.
But Memorilla made the connection from just 16 tokens.
And I asked Claude to write 150 short chats from a madeup user called Sam.
For example, in one chat, Sam mentions being vegan while asking about alternatives to a leather jacket.
And later, I asked, "What should I cook for my parents this Sunday?" And I also added one easy control question, Sam's sister's name and birthday, which was stated plainly in a single chat.
And then I compared four methods, all using the same Quen 3 model.
The second one is a rag with five most similar chats.
The third one has the full chat history in the prompt, and the fourth one is using memorilla.
And it said that Sam's sister is called Emily and was born on April 12th when in the chat it clearly had a different name and a different birthday.
When I gave Memorilla only the one chat about the sister, it got the name Priya right, but the birthday was still wrong.
So my guess is that squeezing a whole chat into one vector keeps the general gist but loses the precise details and that information fades as your history grows.
But the good news is that the repo lets you train your own memory module on your own documents and questions without changing any code.
Because no matter how big your history gets, the model only ever reads those 16 tokens.
I asked the same question over a growing pile of 250 token messages from one all the way up to 512, which is about 128,000 tokens.
And with everything in the prompt, the answer time went from about third of a second to a little over 19 seconds, which is very close to the paper stated 20 seconds.
And Memorilla's answering time stayed basically flat at around 0.12 seconds.
And once you count that in, Memorilla took about 3.2 seconds at 512 documents.
So, it's still about six times faster, just not the 27 times faster that the paper numbers suggest.
The whole book is about 72,000 tokens in size.
And technically, it's too big for Quen 3's model's normal context window.
And when I ran this test, the full context version got five out of eight plot questions, right?
Even though it could only see the second half of the book, while Rag got four and Memorilla got just one.

The idea behind it is a really good one because a memory that always costs the same 16 tokens no matter how much you throw at it would solve a real problem for anyone building an assistant with a long history.
But the good news is that the speed promise actually holds up because the answering time stayed flat even when it had to deal with 128,000 tokens of text.
Memorilla: Latent Semantic Memory for LLMs
The code is based on our paper *[Memorilla: Latent Semantic Memory for LLMs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.21375)*.

A frozen LLM can only use what fits in its context window, so Memorilla reads an entire document collection, such as a user's past chats or a long book, and hands the LLM just 16 memory tokens that carry what each question needs.
With this small budget, it achieves the best average performance against methods such as Mem0 and MemoRAG, and on FactKG it is even more accurate than giving the LLM every document (84.33% vs.
Furthermore, Memorilla can also help an agent keep learning from its own history, raising its average success rate on TextWorld games from 18.6% to 24.2%.

Here is an example from the PersonaMem-v2 test set.
The user has had 107 earlier conversations with an assistant, about 32,000 tokens in total, and now asks a new question.
Memorilla reads all of the conversations and hands them to a frozen Qwen3-8B as just 16 memory tokens, about 2,000 times fewer.
You need one 80 GB GPU, and the first run downloads about 25 GB of models and the 37 MB test set.
row = load_split("pmv2", "test", ensure_data("pmv2", ["test"]))[73] # one user's question and past conversations

model = MemoryVLLM.from_pretrained("memorilla/Memorilla-Qwen3-8B", "pmv2") # Qwen3-8B, the memory module and the encoder answer = model.answer(row["question"], row["documents"], system_prompt=PERSONA_PROMPT) print(f"Question: {row['question']}\nMemorilla: {answer}") ```

> > **Memorilla:** Since you’ve got a family history of type 2 diabetes, you might enjoy breakfasts that balance > protein, healthy fats, and fiber to keep you full without spiking blood sugar—like scrambled eggs with avocado and a > side of roasted veggies, or Greek yogurt with chia seeds and berries.
The only clue is in one of the 107 conversations, where they > asked whether diabetes on the mother's side of the family raises a person's risk more than on the father's side.
> Memorilla connects that clue to a breakfast question that has nothing to do with it, while Qwen3-8B without the > memory answers with a generic list of breakfasts.
Because the LLM always receives the same **16 memory tokens**, no matter how many documents are stored, the approach can potentially scale to millions of tokens.
In the paper, Memorilla compresses books and movie scripts from NarrativeQA by **more than 4,000x**.

On one H100, growing a collection from 1 to **512 documents (about 128K tokens)** leaves Memorilla's response time at **0.74 seconds**, while putting all the documents in the prompt slows the model down from 0.75 to **19.9 seconds, 27x slower**.
The decoder always reads the same 16 memory tokens, so its cost does not depend on the number of documents.
The figure shows it on one B200 GPU for up to four million documents, about one billion tokens at 250 tokens per document.
By default, the memory module processes all document embeddings again for every question, which takes 74 ms for one million documents.
A question then takes 8.1 ms for one million documents and 33 ms for four million, and `torch.compile` brings the one-million case down to 5.0 ms.
The cache takes four times the memory of the embeddings, 80 GiB for four million documents, which still fits on one GPU.
Its memory tokens match the default up to bfloat16 rounding, and FactKG accuracy stays within 0.06 points of the default.

```python model = MemoryVLLM.from_pretrained("memorilla/Memorilla-Qwen3-8B", "pmv2", memory_cache=True, compile_memory=True) collection = model.write(row["documents"]) # encodes the documents and caches the memory module's keys and values answer = model.answer(row["question"], collection, system_prompt=PERSONA_PROMPT) ```

On 4 H100 80GB GPUs, the three stages take about 19 hours and download about 310 GiB of data and embeddings, and evaluating a checkpoint on all eight benchmarks takes about 15 minutes on one GPU.
The trained memory modules are on Hugging Face at [`memorilla/Memorilla-Qwen3-8B`](https://huggingface.co/memorilla/Memorilla-Qwen3-8B).
All were trained with the Qwen3-8B decoder and the Qwen3-Embedding-4B encoder, the defaults of `train.py` and `evaluate.py`.
PersonalizationV4 (PV4) is a synthetic personalisation benchmark released with Memorilla.
